title: if with init, the one for, switch without fallthrough, labels
summary: Go has one loop (for), an if that can declare variables for its own scope, and a switch whose cases never fall through unless you say so.

examples.title: if with an init statement, and switch without break

annotations.note: Handle the error and return early. The happy path stays at the left margin instead of nesting inside else branches.
A switch with no tag is a tidier if/else-if chain: cases are tested top to bottom and the first true one wins.
The init statement declares v and ok for the if and its else only. The comma-ok form tells a missing key apart from a stored zero.
Cases end on their own: no break, and no accidental fall-through as in C or Java. One case can list several values.
fallthrough jumps into the next case body without testing its condition, which is why the second line prints. It must be the last statement in a case; real code rarely needs it.

examples.title: One for for everything, labeled break, per-iteration variables

annotations.note: Since Go 1.22, range accepts an integer and counts 0..n-1.
A for with only a condition is Go's while loop; with nothing at all it loops forever.
A label names the outer loop, so break outer leaves both loops at once. No flag variable, no goto.

Since Go 1.22 every iteration has its own i, also in the three-clause form, so the closures print 0 1 2. A module whose go.mod says go 1.21 or older still gets the old shared variable and prints 3 3 3.

use_cases: if v, err := f(); err != nil { ... } for errors that matter only in this branch
Tagless switch for range checks and classification
for range over slices, maps, strings, channels, integers and iterator functions
strengths: One loop keyword covers counting, while, infinite and range loops; less syntax to remember than C's for/while/do-while
Cases never fall through by accident, the bug Java and C need break (and linters) to prevent
Init statements keep helper variables scoped to the branch that uses them
weaknesses: No ternary operator: a one-line choice becomes a four-line if/else
switch is not exhaustive over iota constants or interface types; the compiler never warns about a missing case
The loop-variable fix depends on the go version in go.mod, so old modules keep the old behavior

pitfalls.title: break inside switch inside for
pitfalls.detail: A plain break in a switch case leaves the switch, not the loop. Label the loop and break the label.
pitfalls.good: loop: for { switch { case done: break loop } }

pitfalls.title: Assuming per-iteration variables in an old module
pitfalls.detail: The Go 1.22 loop semantics follow the go line in go.mod. Code in a module declaring go 1.21 still shares one variable across iterations.

pitfalls.title: Reading a missing map key without comma-ok
pitfalls.detail: m[k] returns the zero value for a missing key, indistinguishable from a stored zero. Use v, ok := m[k] when the difference matters.

quiz.q: In Go, what happens at the end of a switch case body?
options: Execution falls through to the next case
quiz.why: Cases never fall through unless the body ends with fallthrough.

quiz.q: for i := 0; i < 3; i++ { fs = append(fs, func() int { return i }) } in a module declaring go 1.27. What do the closures return?
quiz.why: Since Go 1.22 each iteration has its own i.

quiz.q: How do you leave two nested loops at once?
options: A label on the outer loop and break label
quiz.why: break and continue accept a label naming an enclosing loop.

further_reading.title: The Go Programming Language Specification: For statements
The Go Programming Language Specification: Switch statements

body:
## Concept

Go keeps three control structures and makes each do more. `if` and `switch` accept an
init statement whose variables live only in that statement. `switch` evaluates cases top
to bottom, stops at the first match and never falls through by default; without a tag it
replaces if/else-if chains. `for` is the only loop: three-clause, condition-only (while),
bare (forever) or `range`. Labels let `break` and `continue` target an outer loop.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- C/Java: no parentheses around conditions, braces are mandatory, and `switch` needs no
  `break`. There is no `do-while` and no ternary `?:`.
- Python: `range` over an integer works like `range(n)`; labeled `break` covers what
  Python does with flags or `for/else`.
- JS: the Go 1.22 loop variable behaves like `let` in a JS `for` loop (one binding per
  iteration). The pre-1.22 behavior was JS's `var`.

## Design notes

Use the init form when a value only matters for one branch (`if err := f(); err != nil`).
Return early on errors instead of nesting the success path in `else`; this is the shape
most Go code has, and reviewers expect it. Prefer a tagless `switch` over long
if/else-if chains. Keep `fallthrough` for the rare case where one case is a strict
superset of the next, and leave a comment when you use it.
